He started sorting them on the long table. Big ones here, small ones there. Then he picked up a huge golden sun mask and almost dropped it. It weighed almost nothing! Next to it sat a small plain white mask that felt heavy as a brick in his hand.

Dylan had signed up for the community center band class on a Tuesday, mostly because his best friend Rico had dared him to. Now it was Thursday, and he was staring at a sheet of paper covered with black dots stacked on five lines like ants on a ladder. "That's the staff," said Marisol, the girl next to him, tuning her trumpet. "The dots tell you which notes to play." Dylan squinted. The whole concept felt like a secret code everyone else had cracked except him.

"When do we actually play music?" he whispered.

"When you can find middle C without whimpering," she whispered back.

Rico leaned over. "I found it. It's the dot by itself, in the middle of nowhere. Like a lost sock."

Dylan persevere anyway, even when the trumpets blatted and the drums thundered and the whole room sounded like a garage falling downstairs. He could not hear his own guitar half the time, so his fingers kept landing one beat late. Every Thursday, same problem.

Then came the Thursday of the broken door. The drum room down the hall had a steel radiator pipe running along the wall, and the door had swollen shut in the rain, trapping the drummers inside. While the teacher and a custodian argued about hinges, Dylan noticed something strange. When he pressed his hand on the pipe, he could feel the drummers practicing, a faint buzz in the metal. And when he put his ear against it, he heard the beat clearly, before he heard it again a moment later through the air of the hallway, softer and late, like an echo that hadn't been invited.

He tried it three times to be sure. Ear to pipe, one clear beat. Ear off pipe, the fuzzy air version arriving after. It wasn't his imagination. It wasn't magic either. He thought about the fact he'd read somewhere, that sound traveled about four times faster through water than through air, and about fifteen times faster through steel. That was why an ear pressed to a rail heard a distant train before the sound arrived through the air. The pipe was doing the same job as the rail, carrying the drumbeat down the hall ahead of the sound drifting through the doorway.

"Dylan," said Marisol, "why is your face on the radiator?"

"Because the radiator is punctual." He tapped the pipe with the class's claves, and Marisol leaned in and heard it too, the tap arriving twice, once through the steel and once, dragging behind, through the air.

The door finally popped open, and the drummers spilled out looking like freed prisoners. The teacher said, "Everyone, ears open. Counting is not a voluntary activity. You count or you're lost."

Dylan picked up his guitar. He'd found the trick: when the drums got loud, he watched the drummer's stick hit, and he remembered the pipe, the beat that traveled fastest and arrived first. He played the next line clean, right on time, every dot on the ladder landing where it belonged.

Rico nudged him. "Lost sock found?"

"Delivered by express steel," Dylan said, and struck the last chord.

Anthony and Marisol looked at each other and sprinted for the kitchen sink.

Zoey spread her chemistry notes across Priya's kitchen table, though most of her attention had drifted to the pot on the stove, where the rice had been bubbling for what felt like an hour and still tasted like tiny stones when she pinched a grain. "Your stove is broken," she decided.

"It is not broken," Priya said. "It's just a slow stove. Rice always takes forever here." She said it the way people say things they have said their whole lives, and Zoey wondered how many years of complaints it would take to perpetuate a belief like that, one dinner at a time, until nobody in the house questioned it anymore.

Zoey got up and stood over the pot. The water was boiling, sure, rolling along gently, but something about it bothered her. She had read a page in her textbook that morning, a small paragraph she had almost skipped, and now the words floated back to her. Water's boiling point depended on air pressure. At twice normal pressure, like inside a pressure cooker, water boiled at about 120 degrees Celsius, and food cooked faster. On a high mountain, water boiled well below 100 degrees, so rice and pasta took longer to soften. She looked at Priya's grandmother's old pressure cooker, sitting fat and gleaming on the top shelf, and then at the stubborn pot.

"Can we use that?" she asked.

Priya hesitated. "It's from the old apartment. Nobody's touched it since we moved. Honestly, the difference between stoves is probably negligible." But she got it down anyway, and they scooped the half-hard rice into it with a fresh cup of water, clamped the lid, and set it on the burner. The kitchen clock ticked above them, its brass pendulum swinging in slow, even arcs, and they sat at the table and watched the pot the way you watch weather. After ten minutes, hiss and steam and all, Zoey opened it and lifted out a forkful. The rice was soft. Completely, perfectly soft, and faster than the open pot had managed in forty.

"I changed one thing," Zoey said, mostly to herself. "Same rice, same water, same stove. The only difference was the sealed lid." She was thinking out loud now, turning the pieces over. If the open pot's water was boiling but the rice stayed hard, then boiling alone wasn't the point. It had to matter which boiling, the cooler kind or the hotter kind. "The lid traps the steam, the pressure builds, and the water inside must get hotter before it can boil. That's why the rice gave up."

"So my stove was never slow," Priya said. "My grandmother knew this the whole time."

Zoey laughed and copied the whole thing into her notes, drawing the pot with arrows and labels, because there was a quiz on states of matter next week and this felt like something she would never forget now. They ate the rice straight from the pot with butter and salt, standing at the counter, and Priya put the pressure cooker back on the shelf but turned its handle to face outward.

"Grandma's going to ask why dinner was so fast tonight," Priya said.

"Tell her a chemistry student borrowed her pendulum clock's patience," Zoey said, and took the last forkful.

Hunter had been staring at the same eight lines of code for twenty minutes, and the turtle on Marcus's screen still refused to draw a square. It drew a triangle, paused, then wandered off the edge of the canvas like it had somewhere better to be. "It's the loop," Marcus said, chewing a pen cap. "It has to be the loop."

"Maybe." Hunter leaned closer. The program told the turtle to turn right four times, but the angle said 120 instead of 90. He'd changed three things at once already, the color, the speed, the angle, and now he couldn't remember which version had worked least badly. "Okay, new rule. One thing at a time." He set the angle back to 120, the value from the very first attempt, and changed only the number of repeats from three to four. He ran it. The turtle drew a hexagon. Wrong, but wrong in a new way, which felt almost like progress.

"See, that's the thing," Marcus said. "When you change one thing, at least you learn something from it being wrong."

Hunter changed the repeats back to three and the angle to 90, watching the screen instead of his hands. The turtle drew a clean, boring square. He sat back, grinning. "So it was never the loop count by itself. It was the angle and the count together. You have to mess with one thing, or you're just guessing."

Before Marcus could answer, his laptop chimed with an email. He opened it and laughed. "Oh man. Remember that game site we signed up for last summer? I clicked forgot password, and they just emailed me my actual password. PixelWolf22. The whole thing."

Hunter's grin faded. Something about that tickled the back of his brain, a thread he couldn't quite pull. "Wait. They emailed you your password. Your old one."

"Yeah. Convenient, right?"

"No, that's the opposite of convenient." Hunter pulled the laptop toward him and read the email again, as if the words might rearrange themselves. "Think about what that means. They have to have it stored somewhere, the real one, to send it. Good sites don't do that. They keep a scrambled version, a hash, and you can't turn it back into the password. That's why everywhere else makes you reset it instead of just telling you what it was."

Marcus squinted. "So every site that makes me invent a new password is doing it right?"

"Every site that can't send you the old one," Hunter said. "The ones that can, they're storing it wrong." He said it twice in his head because it deserved saying twice. It was like debugging, he realized. The site had just shown them its source code without knowing it: an email containing a plaintext password was a symptom, and the bug was somewhere underneath, in how the whole thing was built. "You don't fix the symptom. You fix what's causing it."

"So what do I do, close my account?"

"Change your password on it, for starters, and don't reuse PixelWolf22 anywhere that matters." Hunter pushed the laptop back. Then, feeling cordial about the whole afternoon, he added, "And you can keep the square. My treat."

Marcus copied the code into a file and named it HunterIsRightForOnce.py. "One thing at a time," he said, and hit run.

The argument started over the vending machine, which had eaten Olivier's dollar and given him nothing, and which Declan declared was proof that the whole school was being run for the profit of companies that didn't care whether students starved. Olivier had only said that the machine probably wasn't the best evidence, and somehow by lunch they had scheduled a formal debate for Friday, in front of the whole Grade 10 science class, on the topic of climate change and who was actually responsible.

Declan's position, delivered with the confidence of someone who had watched three documentaries over the weekend, was that the greenhouse effect itself was a scam, a story invented so that governments could tax people and so that the vending machine company could keep selling things. Olivier spent Wednesday evening at the kitchen table with his laptop, and his mother kept drifting past with tea and opinions. He found a line in a textbook's first chapter that made him sit up. Without any greenhouse effect at all, Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius instead of roughly 15. He read it twice, then copied it onto an index card and underlined nothing, because underlining was a foible of Declan's, not his.

The interesting thing, Olivier thought as he walked to school Thursday, was that Declan was half right, and that the half he was right about was the boring half. Nobody had invented the greenhouse effect. It was natural, ancient, older than the vending machine and older than every government combined. The part that had changed, the part worth arguing about, was how strong it had become. He wondered whether you could win an argument by agreeing with your opponent first, the way a judo throw works by going with the pull. The question kept him so absorbed that he walked past the school entirely and had to double back through the parking lot, where the custodian was mulching leaves and the smell of wet grass hung in the cold air.

Friday arrived with sleet. Ms. Okoye, who supervised these debates partly out of duty and partly, Olivier suspected, out of amusement, arranged the desks in a horseshoe and reminded everyone that points were awarded for substance, not volume. "Substantive claims, gentlemen," she said, and Declan, who had prepared eleven pages, grinned like a man who had already won.

"The greenhouse effect," Declan began, "is a hoax designed to control people. If it were real, why do they call it an effect? Effects aren't real things." It was not Olivier's job to point out the flaws in that reasoning, so he didn't, and instead he opened with the card from his kitchen table. "You're right that the greenhouse effect is natural," he said, and the room made a small surprised noise, because debaters were supposed to disagree immediately, that was the whole sport. "Without it, Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius instead of roughly 15. Minus eighteen. That's the natural effect. So the effect isn't the problem, and it isn't a hoax, and I'm not going to pretend it is, because that would be lying to you and also to myself."

Declan flipped through his eleven pages, and the flipping was where things went wrong for him, because his pages were all about the effect not existing, and Olivier had just agreed that it existed, which nullified roughly nine of the eleven. "Wait," Declan said. "So you're saying it's real?" "I'm saying it's real and natural and I'm grateful for it," Olivier said. "The question isn't whether it exists. The question is what we've done to it." Declan looked at his pages again, and the class watched him do it, and Ms. Okoye wrote something in her book that was probably a score and was probably generous.

But here was the part Olivier had actually thought about on the walk home through the sleet, and it was the part that didn't fit neatly on an index card. The number on the card, fifteen degrees, was an average, and an average was a kind of summary that could hide more than it showed. It couldn't tell you which fields dried out or which neighborhoods flooded or which winters stopped coming, and it couldn't tell you who owned the vending machine. He had won the debate, or thought he had, and he still couldn't say exactly how much of the problem was Declan's imaginary conspiracy, how much was ordinary people like Olivier feeding the machine their dollars, and how much was just the weather doing what weather had always done, only slightly more of it. The class voted, Ms. Okoye declared a result, and Declan came over afterward, held out his eleven pages, and said, "You can keep these. I'm going to write new ones." "About what?" Olivier asked. "About who owns the vending machine," Declan said, and his eyes had the gleam of a boy who had just discovered that the world contained questions with answers that could be looked up, one of which was standing right there in the cafeteria, humming, with his dollar still inside it.

Dmitri's basement smelled like cold pizza and overheated laptop, and Nathaniel had been staring at the same seventeen lines of Python for forty minutes. The program was supposed to simulate coin flips, and it did, technically, except that every single run of ten flips came out identical: heads, tails, heads, heads, tails, heads, tails, tails, heads, tails. Same order, every time. He leaned back on the sagging couch and said, "If I flip an actual coin ten times, I'd bet anything I couldn't repeat the sequence."

"Then why does the computer do it?" Dmitri was lying on the carpet with his phone held above his face, which was his way of supervising. "Maybe it's broken. Maybe you broke it."

"I didn't break anything. I typed what the tutorial said." Nathaniel tapped the trackpad and ran it again, watching the same ten results scroll past like a train arriving on schedule. Something about it itched. He copied the line that seeded the random number generator, the one with a number stuck in the parentheses, and deleted the number, leaving the parentheses empty, half sure the whole thing would crash. It didn't. The results changed, and changed again, and again, each run different, messy, human-looking. "There," he said. "Fixed."

Dmitri sat up, which for Dmitri was a gesture of enormous respect, and they ran it a hundred times, then a thousand, watching the tallies of heads and tails hover near equal. Then Dmitri's older brother Rafa came downstairs smelling of rain, dropped a duffel bag by the washing machine, and looked over Nathaniel's shoulder long enough to ruin everything. "You see that?" He pointed at the screen, where a stretch of five heads in a row sat embedded in the output like a thread in fabric. "Five heads. That's a hot coin. Next one's tails for sure, that's how it evens out. I've been playing darts on this exact principle."

Nathaniel looked at the five heads, then at the flip that followed them, which was, in that particular run, another head. "But that one came up heads."

"That's why you double your bet when it doesn't," Rafa said, with the serenity of a man explaining gravity to a bird.

After Rafa went upstairs with his laundry, Nathaniel couldn't leave it alone, because two explanations were sitting in front of him and only one could be right. Either the coin, or in this case the program, kept some kind of memory, pulling the next flip toward whatever would balance the streak, or each flip simply didn't care what came before. He wrote a new program, small enough that he understood every line: every time a run of five identical results appeared, it would record what came next. He ran it through thousands upon thousands of flips, and the counts after streaks of heads came out almost exactly half heads and half tails, no different from the counts after anything else. The streak predicted nothing. Which meant it couldn't implicate the coin of anything; it wasn't evidence of a plan or a debt being repaid, it was just a stretch of road.

"So Rafa's wrong," Dmitri said, peering at the numbers.

"About that part, yeah." Nathaniel scratched his head, feeling the second half of the problem arrive like a delayed guest. "Except he did see five heads in a row. That happened. So how real is that?" He widened the program to track whole sequences of a hundred flips, and there it was: nearly every hundred-flip sequence contained a run of five or more identical results somewhere. Five in a row wasn't a miracle demanding an explanation. It was practically guaranteed to show up if you flipped long enough, the way any long text practically guarantees the word "the." Rafa hadn't noticed a rare event; he'd noticed an ordinary one and built a whole betting strategy on it. Nathaniel felt a small, bright shift in how he saw the world, as if a window he'd been looking through had been wiped.

He printed the results, both programs side by side, and carried the paper upstairs to the laundry room, where Rafa was pulling a hoodie out of the dryer. "One hundred flips, and look, the next flip after five heads is still a coin toss. Exactly half. But the five-in-a-row itself shows up in almost every hundred." He held out the page. "So you'll see streaks all night. They just don't mean anything's due."

Rafa took the paper and studied it with the frown of a man checking a restaurant bill. Downstairs, the washing machine thumped into its spin cycle, and Nathaniel waited, oddly hopeful, watching Rafa's thumb move down the column of numbers.

"You wrote this?" Rafa said finally.

"This afternoon. It's my first real program."

Rafa folded the paper in half, tucked it into the duffel bag, and said, "Show me the part where you typed it."

The error message had been on Antoine's screen for eleven minutes, and he had read it maybe forty times. Missing semicolon, line fourteen. He knew the rule; he'd copied it off the board that morning, semicolons end statements in this language the way periods end sentences, and still he had forgotten one, and the machine had refused him entirely. Around him the lab hummed with the particular patience of twenty computers and fifteen students who all wanted to be somewhere else.

"You're staring," said Priya, leaning over from the next terminal. "It's a semicolon. It's always a semicolon."

"It's not always a semicolon."

"Fine. It's usually a semicolon." She tapped his screen with a pencil, an act of unnecessary violence against the glass. "Line fourteen. There."

He typed it. He pressed run. The little program woke up, asked his name, asked his favorite number, and then told him that his favorite number squared was forty-nine, which would have been flattering if he had entered seven. He had entered nine. Somewhere in the arithmetic he had written his own name into the multiplication, some echo of the first example they'd been shown, and the machine had done exactly what he said rather than what he meant. That was the part nobody had prepared him for. The machine was never wrong. It was only ever obedient.

He fixed it, ran it again, and then, because class had ten minutes left and Mr. Okafor had said the early finishers could work on anything, he opened a new file and started to build something small and private: a program that would keep score. Every time he opened the app on his phone, he would tap whether the first video he saw made him feel angry, and the program would tally it. He didn't have a reason he could say out loud. It was only that his evenings had begun to feel like weather, and he wanted a thermometer.

"Is that for the class?" Priya asked.

"Sort of. It's a counter."

"For what?"

"Never mind. It's dumb."

"It's not dumb if it compiles," she said, which was the closest thing to a benediction anyone had offered him all week.

He kept the tally through Thursday, and Thursday told him something. The mornings started gentle, a man restoring an old clock, someone's grandmother making bread. By the seventh or eighth video his thumb had learned a rhythm, and the rhythm brought him arguments, and the arguments brought him faces he already knew he disliked, and each one held him longer than the bread had. His own numbers, laid in a column, were not subtle. Saturday morning he showed Priya the column in the cafeteria, holding the phone between the two trays.

"So your app gets angrier the more you scroll," she said.

"Or I do."

"That's the annoying part, isn't it. You can't tell from inside." She stole one of his fries, which was her way of thinking. "My cousin says the apps pick what keeps you watching. Like, whatever you watch longest, you get more of."

He turned that over while she ate. It would explain the column without requiring him to be an angrier person than he believed he was, and it had the shape of something he'd learned in the lab: the system did what it was told, and what it was told was watch time. Not truth, not usefulness. Watch time. It wasn't a conspiracy; it was a missing semicolon at the scale of a billion people, an obedience so literal it could eviscerate your whole evening and call it success.

But he was honest enough to pause there, because a suspicion that fits your data can still be a story you tell yourself. If he decided the feed was doing this, he'd stop checking his own temper, and that felt like cheating. "I don't know how I'd prove it," he said. "If I only count what the app shows me, I'm being tautological. The app is my whole evidence."

"Then count something the app doesn't touch," Priya said. "Ask me. Ask people. Video call your mom and ask her if you seem worse on Saturdays than Sundays."

"That's not exactly science."

"It's not exactly not science. It's like, epistemology for people with phones." She said it lightly, but he wrote it on his napkin anyway, because the word gave him a handle for the thing he'd been circling all week: what you're allowed to conclude, and from what.

On Sunday he added a second column to his program, one he filled by hand: how he'd felt before opening the app, not after. The two columns sat side by side in the file, and he looked at them for a long time without deciding what they added up to. The machine would run whatever he wrote next. He moved the cursor to the empty line and typed the first semicolon.

story:
Elijah opened his grandfather's laptop on the kitchen table, between a bowl of peach pits and a crossword folded to the sports section, and typed his first line of real code: print("hello"). Nothing happened. Then a lot happened, all of it red, because he had typed the parenthesis with a curly bracket and the interpreter wanted to discuss this at length.

The house smelled like cedar and coffee gone cold hours ago. His grandmother was in the garden pulling tomato volunteers, and through the window he could hear her narrating to the cat, who did not care. Elijah had three weeks before orientation, and a plan he'd told no one: learn enough programming before the fall semester that he wouldn't sit in the first lecture feeling like everyone else had been given a secret handbook. He'd gotten a used laptop from his cousin, a beginner's course saved offline, and one promise from himself, which was to debug before panicking.

He found the bracket. The screen said hello. He raised both fists above his head like he'd sunk a free throw, and his grandmother, glancing in, clapped dirt off her hands and applauded anyway, which made it better, not worse.

By the third day he could write a loop that counted to ten and a little program that converted his grandmother's Celsius canning chart into Fahrenheit, which she declared "a miracle, absolutely a miracle, Elijah," and taped to the refrigerator beside a magnet shaped like a duck. He was learning that syntax was like grammar in a language where a missing comma could make the whole sentence get up and leave the room. Each error message was less an insult than a clue. That felt new. In school, being wrong had always ended in a grade; here, being wrong was the beginning of a hunt, and the hunt was, embarrassingly, fun.

On the fifth day he hit a wall. He was trying to build a page, just a tiny one, a birthday list for his grandfather, when the tutorials kept mentioning that the Web had almost been something else. He went digging, and in an old article on his grandfather's shelf of computer magazines, found it: the first web page had gone online in 1991 at CERN, and its inventor, Tim Berners-Lee, had persuaded the lab to release the underlying technology royalty-free in 1993. Elijah read it twice. Royalty-free. He'd assumed the Web was like television, something built by companies and sold to him in packages. Instead somebody had made it and then, on purpose, given away the right to charge for it. He felt a strange foreboding and excitement at once, the kind you get standing at the edge of a pool you've decided to jump into.

He carried the magazine out to the porch, where his grandfather was doing nothing with great discipline. "Did you know the Web could have been a paid product?" Elijah asked. "Like, you could have paid for every page."

His grandfather considered this with the gravity of a man deciding on a chess move. "I'd have paid," he said. "I pay for the channel with the fishing shows. I'd have paid for anything, back then. I was very lonely in 1993."

"That's not the point, Grandpa."

"It's a little the point." He tapped the magazine. "So the man gave it away."

"He persuaded them to. The lab could have charged."

His grandfather nodded slowly, and Elijah watched a thing happen behind his eyes, some old file being retrieved. "There were people at my work," he said, "who wanted to charge for everything. Software, parking, the good stapler. And there were people who gave things away and got famous for it instead. We used to argue about it at lunch. I mostly sided with the stapler people, if you want the truth."

Elijah laughed, and then found he couldn't stop turning the idea over. He'd been learning to code for purely private reasons, to be ahead, to be safe. But here were two ways of thinking about the same thing: build and charge, or build and release, and neither was simply right. The stapler people kept the lights on; Berners-Lee's choice was why a broke eighteen-year-old on a borrowed laptop could build anything at all. His own position was still equivocal, and he decided he was allowed that. He was going into computer science, presumably to make a living, possibly to make a fortune, and also he now wanted to put his birthday-list project online for free so his cousins in Ohio could see it. Both of those wanted things sat in him without shaking hands yet.

The twist arrived on day eight. He'd finally gotten the birthday page working and called his grandfather over to admire it, and his grandfather leaned in, read the first line, and said, "You put my birthday as the fourth of May."

"It is the fourth of May."

"In the program you wrote four slash five. Day slash month. You've told the computer I was born on April fourth."

Elijah stared at the screen. Somewhere in his beautiful, debugged, syntactically immaculate code, he'd reversed the date format, and every birthday on the list was wrong. "That's not a syntax error," he said, half delighted, half horrified. "The program is perfect and completely wrong at the same time."

"Welcome to my whole career," said his grandfather, and patted him on the shoulder.

Elijah fixed it in four minutes, and then sat looking at the little page, free and public and true, his first working thing in the world. He pressed the key to publish it, and outside his grandmother held up a tomato and shouted, "This one's for you, rocket scientist."
